title: The depth, length and breadth of an idea: iyun, ma'amik and the bond of daas
overview:
The *Kuntres HaHispaalus* taught that true excitement about G-d must come from a detailed *hisbonenus*. Chapters 1 and 2 explain what *hisbonenus* is by explaining *chachma*, *bina* and *daas*. *Hisbonenus* is *iyun*: dwelling on an idea until it is known in every part, unlike *girsa*, the glance at a passing car.

Why can't you learn it once and get it? Every idea has breadth, length and depth, like a river whose fast inner current is its essence. The depth is never seen directly: it is reached only through the length and breadth, the way a child adding apples finally *chaps* how to add. *Chachma* too has a depth, like a spring fed by a hidden aquifer, and through the depth of *bina*, the fiftieth gate, one reaches it: it is the same water. That is *ma'amik*, and the *navon* who understands one thing from another. What the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas* is not the learning itself. *Daas* is the bond of feeling, the interest that keeps the *iyun* going in the right place; it narrows where *bina* spreads, and the two depend on each other.

sections.title: What hisbonenus is: the inner side of bina, called iyun
sections.summary: True excitement about G-d has to come from a detailed *hisbonenus* (contemplation), so first one must know what it is: gazing hard into the depth of an idea and dwelling on it until it is understood clearly in every part. That is the inner side of *bina*, which the *Gemara* calls *iyun*.

phrases.en: all the particular ways or types of excitement that are born in the mind, heart, and thought from a *hisbonenus*, according to the different levels of the soul, the five levels of the soul, *nefesh*, *ruach*, *neshama*, *chaya*, *yechida*.

blocks.text:
Chapter 1. We just finished explaining, in chapters 23 and 24, the *Keser* (crown) of *Atzilus*. In chapter 25 the Mitteler Rebbe is going to start explaining how the *Keser* of *Atzilus* is drawn into *Abba* and *Ima*, the *chachma* (wisdom) and *bina* (understanding) of *Atzilus*. But he does not really explain *chachma* and *bina* there, because he already explained them in chapters 1 and 2.

Chapters 1 and 2 serve a double purpose. They explain *chachma* and *bina*, and *daas* (knowledge) as well, as part of the ten *sefiros* (the Divine attributes), and they explain them in order to show how to do *hisbonenus* (contemplation) and how they relate to each other in *hisbonenus*. So now we go back and learn chapters 1 and 2, which we did not do yet, to learn about *Chabad* as part of the ten *sefiros*.

It was already explained at length in a special *kuntres* (tract), and that refers to the *Kuntres HaHispaalus* (the Tract on Ecstasy). There it explains all the particular ways, the types of *hispaalus* (excitement), that are born in the mind, the heart and the thought from a *hisbonenus*, according to the five levels of the soul: *nefesh*, *ruach*, *neshama*, *chaya* and *yechida*.

There it explains that there are two levels of *machshava* (thought): a cold thought and a hot thought. Then there is excitement in the heart, and excitement in the mind, and then the excitement of the inner *ratzon* (will). Those correspond to the five levels of the soul. And it explains that there are five such levels of the animal soul and five of the G-dly soul, with all the details.

But the main point of that *kuntres* is this. What level of *hispaalus* you are going to get is mainly determined by how refined you are, by the root of your soul. But the main thing is that it should be a true *hispaalus*, a true *avoda* (divine service). Whatever level you are on, it should be true; it does not really matter what level you are on. And in order for it to be real, for it to be true, it has to come from a *hisbonenus* in *Elokus* (G-dliness), a detailed *hisbonenus* in *Elokus*.

**Now**: now that we explained that in order to get this excitement about *Elokus*, that we should love and fear G-d as opposed to other things, we have to understand what *hisbonenus* is, so that we will be able to do it: **what it is essentially, and what we should contemplate on.** Once you understand what it means and how to do it, you have to know what to do it on.

That is what the first nine chapters explain. But he begins, in chapters 1 and 2, by explaining *Chabad* (*chachma*, *bina* and *daas*) in order to explain how to do *hisbonenus*.

phrases.he: הוא ענין ההסתכלות החזקה בעמקות הענין

blocks.text:
The nature of *hisbonenus*, its definition, essentially, just like the technical definition: **It means to gaze very deeply, very strongly into the depth of an idea.** That means with your mind's eye; you should really focus in on the idea.

**And you should dwell on it for a long time.** To stand over it means to watch it, to look at it. And for a long time means: let the idea take hold in your mind, turn it over and over, and examine it from every angle in your mind for a long time, **until you understand it clearly, with all of its parts, in minute detail.**

phrases.en: this is the idea of the *pnimiyus* of *bina*,
This is what the *Gemara* calls *iyun*.
like it says in *Gemara*, in *Maseches Sukka*,
One would learn to amass knowledge, one would learn the *girsa*; and the other one would learn in depth.

blocks.text: **This is the idea of the pnimiyus of bina**, the inner side of *bina* (understanding). *Bina* means to learn, and the *pnimiyus* (inner side) of *bina* is to learn until you understand a thing clearly, with all of its parts, as opposed to the external function of *bina*, which is just to understand something at the surface. This process of understanding something clearly is what the *Gemara* calls *iyun* (close analysis).

So now we have our technical definition of *hisbonenus*. *Hisbonenus* is synonymous with in-depth study, with *iyun*: to make yourself understand, to examine an idea very well until you understand it clearly with all of its parts and details. That is the *pnimiyus* of *bina*, as opposed to *girsa* (knowing the text by rote), just learning on the surface level, which is the *chitzoniyus* (outer side) of *bina*.

As it says in *Maseches Sukka*: there were two sages. **One would learn to amass knowledge**, he would learn the *girsa*, **and the other one would learn in depth.**

So now he explains the difference between *girsa* and *iyun*. Both are *bina*, because any type of learning is a process of *bina*: you are analyzing something, studying it, making yourself understand. But if you only understand superficially, just the surface, that is not the main thing of *bina*. The main thing of *bina* is to be able to really understand into a thing, to know all of its little details and all of its parts; to know the details, as opposed to just getting a general idea of it.

sections.title: Girsa: understanding at first glance, like a car going by
sections.summary: *Girsa* is understanding at first glance, flowing on without stopping, like noticing a car drive past: soon forgotten, and all one can tell is "I saw a car." A *sevara* glanced at with the mind is the same, and so is a world walked through without stopping to see G-dliness in it.

phrases.en: the meaning of *girsa*,

phrases.he: הוא רק הבנת הדבר בהשקפה ראשונה,
phrases.en: is just to understand something according to one's first glance.
that you continue on, and you flow onto the next thing very quickly.
without pausing or stopping to dwell on it at all, as is known.

blocks.text: **The meaning of girsa is just to understand something according to one's first glance.** You look it over once, and whatever idea you get, that is it. And then you flow onto the next thing very quickly, **without pausing or stopping to dwell on it at all.** *Girsa* means you learn quickly, just to cover ground: you learn it once, you get the basic idea, and you go on.

blocks.text: This is like a *mashal* (analogy) of somebody who looks at something with his eye, just glances at it. He does not contemplate at all what he is seeing, **how it works and what it is, with all of its parts, its internal parts and its external parts.** He just glances at it in a passing way.

blocks.title: A car drives by
blocks.text: You are walking down the street and some car drives by. Okay, so you know it is a car. But you did not stop and examine exactly what kind of car it is, and think about how it works: is it a regular car or a hybrid car, what kind of an engine, how many cylinders might it have? You did not think about all the details.

phrases.he: שבמשך זמן ודאי ישכח עליו לגמרי
phrases.en: that surely as time passes, you'll totally forget that it happened.

phrases.he: וגם לא יוכל לספר לזולתו רק כלליות ענין אותו הדבר
phrases.en: and even right after you see it, you'll only be able to tell somebody else the general thing,
because it was just seen with a passing eye,
that there was no real recognition, real sinking in of the eye at all.

blocks.text: As time passes you will surely forget it totally; it was not really important, and you did not really think about it. And even right after you see it, if somebody asks, "Oh, what did you see?", you will only be able to tell him the general thing: "Oh, I saw a car." You will not be able to tell him the details, **because it was just seen with a passing eye**: there was no real recognition, no real sinking in of the eye at all. Real recognition means knowing all of its little details, until you are intimate with the thing and can recognize it right away.

phrases.he: וכן העברת עין השכל באיזה סברא בהשקפה ראשונה
phrases.en: and the same thing applies to just glancing with your mind at some *sevara* with just the first glance,

phrases.he: בלתי עכוב והעמדה לעיין בו היטב,
phrases.en: without pausing and stopping to examine it well,

phrases.he: ולא ידע בסברא זו לתכליתה כלל
phrases.en: you will not really know the *sevara* in its fullest at all.

blocks.text: The same thing applies to glancing with your mind at some *sevara* (a line of reasoning) at first glance, **without pausing and stopping to examine it well**: you will not really know the *sevara* in its fullest at all. You will have some general idea of it. But to really understand it, what was the question, what was the answer, why are we compelled to say this, why can't we say something else, what is the support for it, to really appreciate all the details, you have to study *b'iyun* (in depth). You have to go in and ask all these questions and find answers, and then ask harder questions, and keep digging until it is really clear.

The same thing with *hisbonenus*. If a person wants to really understand *Chassidus*, he has to learn it *b'iyun*. As the Rebbe says, just as you learn *Gemara b'iyun*, you should learn *Chassidus b'iyun*; you have to really learn it.

And also with the world. If you want to see G-dliness in the world, if you want to study G-d's book, you have to learn it *b'iyun* too. We cannot think that we are just going to walk around in life seeing G-dliness without stopping and thinking about it, trying to really see what is going on in the world around us, noticing *hashgacha pratis* (Divine providence) and these things. That is one of the main ideas of *avoda*: *hisbonenus* not just in the book, but in the world, too. The books are just helping you to do that more properly.

Now, to explain the difference between *iyun* and *girsa*, he will explain that every idea has three dimensions: a length, a width and a depth. This explanation is important because we have an unasked question: why does it have to be so? Why, to understand something properly, do we have to learn *b'iyun*, really go into it, spend time thinking about it, ask questions and examine every detail? Why can't we just learn something once and get it? Let's say we're smart, let's say we're quick. It says in places that it is impossible for a person to understand something properly learning it the first time: your first glance is never going to grasp the depth of the idea. Why not?

And the same with the world around us. "Why isn't it possible for me to walk around and see G-dliness? Why do I have to work, and do *avoda*, and do this *hisbonenus*," learning all this *Chassidus* and doing *hisbonenus* before *davenen* (praying) and during *davenen*? "Why can't I just walk down the street and see it?" That is the unspoken question we are addressing now.

sections.title: Every idea has breadth, length and depth, like a river
sections.summary: Breadth is explaining an idea to every side in many details; length is bringing it down into *meshalim* until a small child can grasp it; depth is its essential point, like the fast inner current of a river from which all the rest of the water spreads. Everything comes from the depth, and the depth is reached only through the length and the breadth.

phrases.he: כי הנה ג' דברים הוא שיש בכל דבר מושכל.
phrases.en: There are three things or three aspects to every idea:
There is the depth of the idea, the length of the idea, and the width of the idea.

blocks.text: For there are three things, three aspects, to every idea: *omek*, *orech* and *rochav*, the depth of the idea, the length of the idea and the width of the idea. Now he explains these three dimensions.

phrases.en: the width

phrases.he: הוא בחינת הסבר המושכל לכל צד בפרטים הרבה
phrases.en: The width of an idea means to explain the idea to every side with a lot of details,
like the width of a river,
and not just saying things like they are in the shortest way,
which would be like a narrow river.

blocks.text: **The width of an idea means to explain the idea to every side with a lot of details, like the width of a river**, and not just saying things as they are in the shortest way, which would be like a narrow river. This kind of analogy carries over even into English: when you say something is a broad idea, that implies that it has a lot of parts, a lot of fields and subjects within it.

blocks.title: Medicine, a broad subject
blocks.text:
You would say medicine is a broad idea, because there are so many different fields in medicine and so many different types of doctors: regular doctors, and specialists, and you can specialize in so many different things, each part of the body. And then there are all these different theories in medicine: Western medicine, Eastern medicine, holistic medicine. Not everybody would agree exactly which ones are included in medicine and which ones are just quackery, but there are all kinds of theories within that one subject.

If you want to say it in the narrowest way, you would just say, "Medicine is the science of healing the body," or something like that, a dictionary definition. That would be like a narrow river. When you start explaining all these different aspects of medicine, you are making the idea much wider. You are broadening the explanation of medicine.

phrases.en: the length

phrases.he: הוא עוצם ירידות ההשכלה להלביש את המושכל במשלים שונים
phrases.en: The length of the idea is a measure of the intensity of the descent of the idea to enclothe it into *meshalim*,

phrases.he: עד להביאו בהשגות התינוק קטן כו',
phrases.en: until you bring the idea to within the grasp of even a small child.
like a river that flows and is drawn out for a long time, a long way.
as explained at length in the *Kesavim*.
about the length of the skins that covered the *Mishkan*.

blocks.text: **The length of the idea is a measure of the intensity of the descent of the idea to enclothe it into meshalim** (analogies), **until you bring the idea to within the grasp of even a small child.** So it is how difficult it is to explain the idea simply. If it is a very deep, very difficult idea, that is very hard; it takes a very talented teacher to put it into simple *meshalim* and make it understandable to a small child.

But an idea that is not so deep is very easy to explain to a child, because it is a child-like idea anyway. If you want to explain, let's say, football, it is not so deep. And something really simple would be tiddlywinks: a really, really little kid could play tiddlywinks. It is a game where you have a little short cup and these flat, round, coin-like discs, and you try to flip the discs into the cup. "That's the whole game. Yeah, that's it, it's pretty short." It is very narrow, too; it does not have very much to it.

blocks.title: One apple plus one apple
blocks.text:
You can see these dimensions when you teach a little kid math. Say you are going to teach him addition. You could give him the whole width, but there are so many different problems and so many examples; that would be the whole width of it. Even when you start with just one idea, one plus one is two, it is just one example, and even that is too abstract. So you have to make it simple and put it in a *mashal*: one apple plus one apple is two apples, one fishy plus one fishy is two fishies. Like that the kid can start to understand what you are talking about.

That is the length: to bring it down from one plus one, the abstract, to one apple plus one apple. That is not such a far descent. But to explain something deeper, putting it into a *mashal* is a farther descent.

There are two things in the length, the potential length and the actual length. The potential length depends on the idea itself: the deeper the idea, the more length it will have. (That is what he will say later, that the width and the length depend on the depth.) But how much length actually comes out depends on how far the teacher and the student are from each other. If the teacher has a very deep understanding and the student a very shallow, low one, the teacher is like a mountain and the student like a little valley, and to go from one to the other the idea has to flow a very long way. That is the *mashal*.
**Like a river that flows and is drawn out for a long time, a long way**: like a river flowing from a mountain. If it is flowing from a high mountain to a low place, that is very, very long.

As explained at length in the *Kesavim*. The *Kesavim*, as it says in *HaYom Yom*, is a name for the Alter Rebbe's longer *maamarim* (discourses): the longest discourses the Alter Rebbe said at the end of his life are called *Kesavim*, manuscripts. So it is explained at length in the manuscripts of the Alter Rebbe's later discourses, **about the length of the skins that covered the Mishkan**.

There it explains the idea of length from the verses about how the skins should be a certain length: it says they should be thirty *amos* long "by the *ama*." Why is it necessary to repeat the word *ama*? It explains that this is the idea of the same thing just being doubled over to make it long. You take the same *ama* of skin, and then you do another one, and another one, and another one, and you attach them to each other, and they fold over, and it becomes long.

This is a *mashal* for an idea that goes from teacher to student, teacher to student. It is really the same idea, but because it goes through many different stops, through many teachers, and each one explains it a little differently, and it goes through their understanding and their minds, you say it went a long way. That is how the idea becomes long. Or even within one teacher: he goes from one explanation and, based on that, to a simpler explanation and a simpler one, and within himself the idea gets applied at lower and lower levels until it becomes a very simple idea. That is also the idea of length.

blocks.text: Then there is the depth: **that's like the depth of a river, that from the depth, that's where it spreads out, but in itself is not wide at all.** What exactly is this depth of the river? **The main identity, the main essence, the main self of the river**, which is called the undercurrent. **This is the main flow of the river from its source.**

blocks.title: The continental divide
blocks.text: The way a river works is that you have some water source, either a spring up in the mountain or a spring combined with melting snow and rainwater that collects from different mountains. In America, for example, there is something called the continental divide. The Rocky Mountains go from Mexico up to Canada and split America; not in half, because they are all the way to the west, but they split it. Any rain that falls to the west of that line will join up into little streams, then into bigger streams, little rivers and bigger rivers, and end up in the main rivers, and it will all flow to the Pacific Ocean. And all the rain that falls on the other side goes the other way. Of all the rainwater that falls on America, some is absorbed into the ground and grows crops, some evaporates back into the air, and the rest flows down and turns into rivers. And then there are springs of water, "which we'll talk about soon."

So the way a river works: the flowing water carves out a path, a little trough, a groove in the ground. At the bottom and sides the water drags against the ground, and on the top it drags against the air. But that makes a kind of cushion, and in the middle the water can flow very fast; it becomes like a lubricated tube. In the middle there is this stream of water that flows very fast, and that is the main flow of the river. The waters on the sides and on the top flow much slower. That is called the undercurrent. Sometimes, if there is a big difference between the top and the middle, it can be dangerous for swimming: it can pull somebody under the water.

This flow is really the main thing in a river: it is flowing, trying to go from the mountains to the ocean. If on the way the land becomes flatter, it will spill over and become wide, and it will also be able to go a long way. If there is not so much water, it will flow a little bit and then get absorbed in the ground and dry up. There has to be a lot of water flowing for it to make it all the way down to the ocean. "So that's the way a river works."

But the main thing is the inner stream that flows very fast, and the water on the sides and the top is just there to help it do that.

blocks.title: When the child chaps how to add
blocks.text:
When you teach children how to add, first you have to take the idea and bring it down into physical examples, one apple plus one apple and one fishy plus one fishy. After a few *meshalim* like that they understand that problem. They understood one idea; that is the length. Now you give them another one: two apples plus two apples is four apples, and they understand that one. You keep giving them a bunch of examples, and they start to understand the difference between the examples and to see a common theme, a common denominator, which is the central point of how to add.

At a certain point they *chap* it (Yiddish: catch it). They grasp that point, and now you do not need to give them any more examples or *meshalim*. They understand that you can add anything: apples or fish or chairs or books, it does not matter, it is the same thing. Just as one plus one is two, two plus two is four and one plus two is three, and they can add any number. They just know how to add. That is the point, that is the depth.

blocks.text: Once you have that, you can bring it into any length automatically. If I ask you, "Can you add apples for me?" you say, "Well, of course I can add apples. What's the difference?" To the essential point it is the same thing, whether you are adding something abstract or something concrete. And if I ask you to add any numbers, even a really big one, a seven-digit number to another seven-digit number, it is not really harder. It is really just adding two numbers over and over again: you have to know the rules, how to add all the numbers and how to carry over. It just takes more work. That is the width: all the different particular problems I could give you, you can add. That is what happens when you get the depth.

So why not just teach the kids the depth? Why teach them the length and the width? This is the main point: it is impossible to grasp the depth without the length and the width. Through studying the length and the width you grasp the depth. The depth itself is beyond; you never see the depth directly, only how it is applied, how it is expressed in these external things, the length and the width.

So on the one hand, how much you have the depth is how much you can bring out the length and the width. And the reverse: the more you study the length and the width, the more you will grasp the depth. "That's the rule." And this is why, if you want to understand an idea, you have to do *iyun*: *iyun* means to study the length and the width to grasp the depth. The more *iyun* you do, the more you get the depth, and the more you will know.

Now back to the parenthesis about the height, that from the idea you go up to understand more. You keep going up, higher and higher, **until you reach the depth of above**, the highest height: **like in the time of the flood of Noach, that the water went higher and higher until it covered everything.**

The same thing will happen spiritually in the time of *Moshiach*, in the five hundredth year of Noach's life. What does that mean? Noach is called a *tzaddik* (righteous man), so he represents the attribute of *yesod*. The attribute of *yesod* corresponds to the sixth millennium, the one we are in now, from the year 5000 to the year 6000, and the five hundredth year of Noach's life means the year 5500. So halfway through the sixth millennium this flood began already, a spiritual flood to prepare the world for *Moshiach*, which is the seventh millennium. The second half of the sixth millennium was already preparing this flood, preparing the world for the time of *Moshiach*.

As it says in the *Zohar* about that time, the gateways of *chachma* opened up, and at that time both the secular and the G-dly knowledge opened up. In the world there was a big boost in the knowledge of science, and the knowledge of *pnimiyus haTorah* (the inner Torah) and *Chassidus* started to spread and open up.

These are the wellsprings of the depth of *chachma* that got stronger, went higher and higher, and covered all the mountains: the geysers that burst forth from the bottom of the earth are the wellsprings of the wisdom. **And the reservoirs of the heavens opened up also**, bringing down the water that is higher than the heavens, which is called the depth of above, **which depends on the depth below, because the beginning is wedged in the end.**

This is explained in two ways. One way is that the depth below, the wellsprings that opened up, is secular knowledge, the knowledge of this world; and the knowledge of the sciences advancing more and more helps to open up the knowledge of G-dliness too, so that we will see G-dliness in the world.

The other explanation, the one Reb Hillel of Paritch gives in his commentary, which is more directly in line with what he is saying here in the book, is this. When a person does *iyun* and works to understand the idea, that is called opening up the wellsprings of *chachma*: you are digging into the earth to bring out the hidden water. You take an idea, delve into it, and try to uncover its hidden depth. When a person does that *iyun*, it automatically opens up his *chachma*, which is higher than the world: he gets a *chiddush* (a new insight), a flash from *chachma*. But for the source of *chachma* to open up and give new ideas, a person has to do the *iyun*, because the end is wedged in the beginning. When you study the idea over and over, that is where you really get its essence, and the essence is really higher than even *chachma*. That is why it will open up the *chachma* itself.

As the verse says, **Either cast your question to the depth, means to go deep, or to raise it up on high.** Those are the two ways to answer your question. In a way they are synonymous, going deep and going high; but you also see that specifically you first have to go to the depth, and afterwards you can raise it up to get the height. First you have to do the *bina*, the *hisbonenus*, and then you will be able to get the *chachma*. So it is explained in the *Kesavim*, in the long *maamar* of the Alter Rebbe.

Back to what we are saying: the length, the width and the height: **it all comes from the essential depth, which is the point of the idea**, the way it flows out from *chachma*. *Chachma* is called *ayin* (nothing): an abstract point, which is like nothing compared to the explanation of *bina*, which is concrete and tangible, a *yesh* (something). As it says, the river went out from *Eden*. The river represents *bina*, which goes out from the wellspring, which is *chachma*: **because bina is called a river**, and that is why it flows out of its source, **and chachma is called the wellspring, the source itself, as is known.**

sections.title: Iyun: dwelling on the idea, a vessel for the depth of bina
sections.summary: *Iyun* is to stand over an idea and study it very much, the opposite of rushing, until one knows it inside and out, which is why *hisbonenus* has a double *nun*. *Iyun* is only a vessel for the depth of *bina*; what the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*, concentration, is not *iyun*, and it helps only after the idea has been studied.

That is called scrutinizing it: **until he knows it very well, he knows it thoroughly, he's totally familiar with it, even all of its internal parts**, and how it works.

blocks.title: The craftsman takes it apart
blocks.text: If you bring something to a craftsman and something in it is broken, you ask him what is broken. He takes the thing, carefully turns it over and looks at it, and then he takes it all apart and examines every piece and evaluates it. He sees what is wrong: whether it just needs to be cleaned, or fixed, or replaced. He lays it all out on the table and sees what is what and exactly what is going on, and he knows everything, all of its details.

blocks.text:
**And this is what is called hisbonenus, with a double nun.** The word *hisbonenus* comes from *bina*; it means to make yourself understand. But it should really have only one *nun*: it should be *hisbinus*. Why is it *hisbonenus*? Grammatically, the double *nun* implies an intense form of the verb. *Hisbinus* would mean *girsa*; *hisbonenus* means *iyun*, to study in depth. It also hints that a person has to go over the idea over and over; that is why there is the double *nun*. You cannot just learn it once, you have to go back and learn it again.

So it is with the double *nun* specifically, because that implies that you are *misbonen* (contemplating) and studying it a lot, to analyze it and really think about it. As Rashi explains *b'iyuni*, what *iyun* means: **to dwell on an idea until you understand it clearly with all its parts.**

blocks.text: It comes out, then, that this *iyun* is only a vessel for the delving of *bina* itself. Based on how we explained the relationship between the length and width and the depth, everything comes out from the depth, so the more you grasp the depth, the more length and width you have: the more you can apply the idea in all sorts of ways and explain it very simply. But on the flip side, if you are a student starting out and you want to grasp the depth, the only way to reach it is by going through the length and the width. The length and the width make a shell around the depth, and you have to crack it, to break through it, to find the depth. The only way to do that is by going through the whole length and the whole width; the more you do that, the more you find the depth behind it.

So **this thing of iyun, of analyzing the subject, is only like a vessel, it's only a tool for the actual delving of bina itself.** What do we mean? *Iyun* is just to spend a lot of time dwelling over the idea, not to pass over it. If you let an idea pass through your mind very quickly, your power of *bina* does not have the chance to really focus on it and "do its magic" to figure it out. But if you hold the idea in your mind for a long time, your faculty of *bina* can analyze it, become sensitive to it, and really find the depth.

Now we go even a little past this. **Seemingly, what we just described as iyun is what the world calls ha'amakas hadaas** (deep concentration). What the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas* is meditation: to concentrate on an idea, to hold it in your mind for a long time, and that focus, that concentration, will automatically bring a flash of inspiration, an idea from *chachma*. That is how it seems. **But this is not true, this is not so.** *Ha'amakas hadaas* is not *iyun*, it is not *hisbonenus*. *Ha'amakas hadaas* **is also only a kli**, only a tool, but it is a tool to come to the true depth of the idea, which is even higher than what *bina* gives you.

In the rest of the chapter he will explain *chachma*, how *chachma* too has a length, width and depth, and how a person can go deeper and deeper into it; and then *daas*, and then we will better understand this relationship between *bina* and *daas*: what *bina* gives you and what *daas* gives you, and how the two have to work together. But the basic idea is that concentration, focusing your mind on an idea, does not actually make you understand the idea. It is studying the explanations that makes you understand the idea.

If you just go and meditate on an idea, or try to focus in on it and attune yourself to it, cultivate a sensitivity to it just by focusing, that will not do anything, at least nothing positive. Later we will say what negative things can happen if a person does that kind of meditation without the *bina* first, without first studying.

But when a person is studying, obviously, if he does not concentrate, is not attentive and does not really put himself into it, he is not going to understand. As the famous *HaYom Yom* says, the main thing in understanding *Chassidus* is that you should feel that it is *noge'a* (relevant) to you, that it relates to yourself.

blocks.title: Rabbi Meir and the woman's chicken
blocks.text: Like the story with the lady with the chicken. It is a story in the *Gemara* that is brought in the *HaYom Yom*. Rabbi Meir was once in the *beis midrash*, and they were discussing a case of a chicken, whether it is kosher or not. He kept bringing all these ingenious arguments to try to say it is kosher, and they kept saying, "No, it's not." Finally they said, "You know, just give it up, man. The chicken is not kosher." They thought he was just really adamant about it, but it was weird: he was coming up with the craziest things to make it kosher, and it just was not kosher. So he said, "I promise you that all of these arguments were told to me by a woman that brought me a chicken."

She was not learned, and not necessarily smart or intellectual, but because it was important to her, because she really wanted the chicken to be kosher, she thought up all these arguments. So too, even a person who is not so smart or knowledgeable, if it really relates to him, if he has a *daas* for it and feels that it connects to himself, will really understand it.

Nevertheless, all these things that relate to *daas*, concentrating, meditating, focusing and connecting yourself to the idea, only help after you have the *bina*, after you study the idea and understand it.

blocks.title: Medical school and internship
blocks.text: This is understood in any discipline. A person in medical school who wants to be a doctor obviously has to study all the explanations of medicine and learn the whole thing, the whole length and width; otherwise there is no way he will really understand it and have the *daas* to really be a doctor. Just picturing the human anatomy, staring at a picture of it, or any kind of meditation like that, will not make a person understand. He has to actually study the books and spend years of studying, and apprenticeship, and internship: the doctor has to do an internship too, to study under another doctor and see how it is actually done. It is not enough to learn it in the books. They have to find some doctor who will let them hang around and be their *mashpia* (mentor) and teach them how to be a doctor.

That is the idea of a *mashpia*. "That's so many things." There are different things in a *mashpia*, but one of the main things is that he is supposed to be your guide and mentor in *avodas Hashem* (the service of G-d).

He will explain more about *ha'amakas hadaas* and *daas* at the end of the chapter. But for now: *bina* only gives you the depth of what is called a *musag*, the idea as it is in *bina*. *Daas* connects you to the *chachma* that is higher than *bina*, but you can do that only after you have the *bina*.

sections.title: Ma'amik: through bina to the depth of chachma, like water traced to its spring
sections.summary: Higher still is *ma'amik*, reaching above *chachma* to its source. *Chachma* too has depth, length and breadth, like a spring fed from a hidden aquifer. The depth of *bina*, the fiftieth gate, seems no match for the depth of *chachma*; but it is the same water, so whoever delves into the *musag* taps its source and draws new *chiddushim* of *chachma* into *bina*.

So you can go from the external understanding of *girsa* to the depth of *bina*, the depth of the understanding: that is what *hisbonenus* does. Then you can go from *bina* to *chachma*: that is what *ha'amakas hadaas* does. Then you can go from *chachma* to the *Keser*: that is what *ma'amik* does. "And we're going to explain all these things."

blocks.text: The answer is that when you do the *hisbonenus* and work to find the source of an idea, meaning that you do the *iyun* in *bina* to try to find the *chachma*, that **will automatically reach up to the root that brings down the flow of the maayan of chachma**, the wellspring of *chachma*. blocks.text: So whatever you want to accomplish, the depth of *bina*, past it to *chachma*, the depth of *chachma*, all the way up to the depth of *Keser*, whatever you want, you want to get the *etzem* (essence): how do you do it? Say you are learning a book, a *maamar*, whatever it is. You take the *sefer* and you have to learn it. And then you have to learn it again, and again, and again, and really work to understand it: not just more times, but more in depth. Ask questions and answer them, learn it with another person to get a fresh perspective, and keep working on it. Imagine you are going to give a class on it to totally skeptical intellectual people who will ask you all these questions: what questions are they going to ask, how am I going to explain it to them? Think what the *nimshal* (what the analogy stands for) is, how you could apply it, what examples there are. Really work on an idea until you really understand it.

blocks.text: The more you just keep working on the idea itself, going over the same words and the same ideas, that *iyun*, that *hisbonenus*, will automatically bring you deeper and deeper. First you get the depth of *bina*, then you start to get the *chachma*, then eventually even the source of the *chachma*. So now you have something to work with: you work with a *yesh*, with the explanations of *bina*, and automatically the *bina* will open up the *chachma* and even the *Keser*. And as he will say in the next chapter, the *bina* also opens up everything under it: the *middos* (emotions) and the *maaseh* (action).

This is the whole *shita* (approach) of *Chabad*: when you do *hisbonenus*, it changes your perspective, it changes your feelings, and it brings you to action. This chapter and the next explain the philosophical grounds for the *Chabad* approach to self-improvement, to *avoda* on yourself. Doing *hisbonenus* will bring you all the way to the source of *chachma*.

**This is called the depths of chachma, or the hidden chachma**, *taalumos chachma*. **For just like there's a length, width, and depth in bina, which like we said before is called a yesh**: what does it mean that it is a *yesh*? That an idea in *bina* is something tangible that you can explain and work with, a particular explanation. Say you are learning a piece of *Gemara* and you learn Rashi, and Rashi explains the *Gemara* to you. His explanation is a *yesh*, a very concrete thing. Tosafos explains it a different way, and that is also a *yesh*.

Or the kid learning math who is told that one apple and one apple are two apples; even the numbers, one plus one is two, are a concrete example, a particular problem. But the concept of math in theory behind it is an abstract point, much harder to talk about. **So too there's a length, width, and depth to the wellspring of chachma, which is called a nothing**, an abstract point.

blocks.title: The underground lake and the mountain spring water
blocks.text:
**What's the depth of the wellspring? The depth of the wellspring is its original root, where it's cut out in the stone deep in the ground.** There is a deep pocket of water under the ground, like an underground lake, and a crack that goes up through the earth's crust, wiggling its way through. The water makes its way through these cracks and veins until it spurts out of the earth somewhere, and that is the *maayan* (wellspring). "And then they bottle it, and they sell it to you as mountain spring water."

**And from there, its flow spreads up until it bursts through the earth, and it comes out drop by drop, and now it's coming revealed from its hidden source.** Under the ground it is hidden: you walk around and you do not see any water. You have to dig down, and if you are in the right place you will find a well. "I think wherever you are if you dig deep enough, you'll hit the water table." But in certain places you do not have to dig that deep; there is a big well.

**And the deeper you go, the more hidden it is**, as it says by the *Mabul* (the Flood) that the wellsprings of the abyss, the very deep underground lakes, burst forth. Certain springs and geysers are normally open, and there are others very deep down that are normally closed; even if you dig a well you are not going to hit them. But in the *Mabul* they all burst forth, and that is how it flooded everything, plus it rained too. **For the earth is riddled with veins**: veins of water and veins of gold and silver and everything. And these veins, now speaking of the water, have a first source. In English that underground lake is called an aquifer. There are big underground lakes, aquifers, and underground rivers flowing between them, and cracks in the ground that bring the water up, and that is where wellsprings come from.

That is the *mashal*. **And this is what it says, that chachma is found from nothing.** What does it mean that it comes out from nothing? From the concealed source of *chachma*, which is called the depth of *chachma*. The underground lake that is the hidden source of the water, deep under the ground, is the depth of *chachma*, the *omek*. Then there is the width of the wellspring: how wide a crack you have in the ground, all the way through until it breaks forth, where you will actually see that there is a wellspring. Then the wellspring drips out and flows down to the river: that is the length, that it goes out from itself to the river. "So now we're going to explain what chachma is."

phrases.he: והחכמה הוא המצאת שכל החדש שיוצא כברק כו'
phrases.en: The power of *chachma* is the ability to find a new idea that comes out like a lightning bolt, like a flash,
as known,

phrases.he: ומקור מחצבו בהעלם עומקו הוא עיקר עצמיות ותוך תוכו

blocks.text: **The power of chachma is the ability to find a new idea that comes out like a lightning bolt, like a flash**: all of a sudden, you are thinking and thinking, and all of a sudden, boom, you get an idea. *Chachma* is like a wellspring: all of a sudden this new thing comes out that you did not see anywhere, because it was hidden under the ground, and all of a sudden this water pops out. So too *chachma* brings out a new idea from its source.

Just as we explained with *bina*, that the main thing is the depth of *bina* and the length and width come out from it, so too **the source where it comes from under the ground**, that big lake of water, **is the main, the main real self, the main etzem of the chachma, and that's its real inwardness**, what is really behind it. In other words, behind the *chachma* is a hidden potential, the *koach hamaskil* (the power of insight): a person has this hidden reservoir of knowledge and of abilities to understand, and it comes out in different ways in the *chachma*.

phrases.en: like we're saying before about the depth of the concept in *bina*,

phrases.he: שאינ' רק העומק של ההשגה דבינה
phrases.en: That's only the depth of the idea the way that it's understood in *bina*,
and it's felt as like a concrete thing, as like a *yesh*,
I understood something with a revealed *sevara*

phrases.he: שעומק של הסבר ההשגה הוא בחינת אין של היש דהשגה בלבד,
phrases.en: because the depth of this explanation of the idea is only the *ayin* of the *yesh*.

phrases.he: ואין לו ערך לגבי אין דחכמה טרם שבא לכלל השגה כלל,
phrases.en: and it's not comparable to the abstract point of *chachma* before it comes into the whole world of understanding.
not even the depth of the explanation of *bina*
the *omek* of *bina* is the distilled essence

blocks.text: Like we said before about the depth of the concept in *bina*: the depth of *bina* we explained is not the true depth, not the deepest depth, not the farthest you can go. **That's only the depth of the idea the way that it's understood in bina, and it's felt as like a concrete thing, as like a yesh**, and you feel, "Oh, **I understood something with a revealed sevara**, that I can explain to you logically with words." The point of *chachma* is beyond that. It is just something you have got to *chap*; you have to find the point behind it, which is much harder to articulate. **Because the depth of this explanation of the idea is only the ayin of the yesh**: only the abstract point you finally get behind all these explanations, but the abstract point of these explanations.

blocks.title: One Rashi, and the point in every Rashi
blocks.text:
Say you are learning *Gemara* and you learn a Rashi, how he explains the *Gemara*. At first you do not really get it, and you review it a few times until you really understand what he is saying: you understand its *chiddush*, his question and his answer. Or in *Chumash*, say you are going to a Rashi *sicha* (talk of the Rebbe on Rashi), and you really understand the Rashi; "the truth is a Rashi sicha is a little bit past that," but say you just learned it, thought about it, and really got it. When you understand that Rashi, that is just the depth of the *bina*: you understand the explanation here.

If you go deeper and start to think into it, you start to get a *chachma*: you start to see how this Rashi really represents a *shita* (system), that there is a point in this Rashi that you find in every Rashi, or at least in many of them.

That is already bringing out a *chachma*, the abstract point, a much deeper and more abstract depth. And then you start to see that there is a *machlokes* (dispute) between Rashi and Tosafos that runs through many arguments, much more abstract than a particular idea, until you find the true depth that is the source of every argument: the way he explains every *Gemara* is because he is looking at it from this point. Sometimes a *sicha* will bring out something like that, "like the Rogatchover sometimes does that." To see it, you have to learn not just one Rashi really well but many, and learn them all very well; when you learn them all *b'iyun*, you start to see it. "Or if you learn a Rashi sicha, then you can cheat."

So with the understanding of just that first Rashi, it is true that you got this abstract depth, you really get the point of the Rashi, which you cannot explain; you have to just learn it and then you really get it. But nevertheless it is still not the real depth, **and it's not comparable to the abstract point of chachma before it comes into the whole world of understanding.**

blocks.title: Koach and poel
blocks.text: The abstract point of *chachma* is before it is applied to any particular instance. Say you know that Rashi has a certain *shita*. Or the *machlokes* between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel: the Rebbe explains it as *koach* (potential) and *poel* (actual), and shows how that explains many different disputes. The idea of *koach* and *poel* is a *chachma*; it does not relate to anything particular. When you come to a particular dispute you have to say, "Okay, so how would I look at it from a *koach* way, how would I look at it from a *poel* way?" But the point of *koach* and *poel* itself does not have to do yet with a particular explanation of a certain case. So not even the depth of the explanation of *bina* is comparable to the *ayin* of *chachma*. The depth of *bina* is its distilled essence, but it is still not as deep as *chachma*.

blocks.question: So seemingly, how is it possible to do hisbonenus, get just the depth of bina, and ever get to chachma?
blocks.text: Because seemingly *bina* just does not reach that far. It only reaches the depth of *bina*; it will not get anywhere near even the outside of *chachma*, let alone the depth of *chachma*.

phrases.en: however,

phrases.he: עומק המושג נקרא שער הנו''ן דבינה,
phrases.en: the depth of understanding, which is called the *shaar hanun* of *bina*,
even though it goes from the abstract point of *chachma* to be a *yesh*,
a wellspring is gonna go out from the *Kodesh HaKodashim*.
It's gonna start out very thin and narrow, like the horns of a grasshopper,

phrases.he: שרשו מגיע בעומק דחכמה הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: its source reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma* that he mentioned before.
and like we see tangibly,
that anybody that just studies and goes deeper into the depth of the *musag*, of the explanation of whatever he's learning,
he taps into the source and the root of the concept the way it's all the way in *chachma*,

phrases.he: להמציא בחינת חדשות דאור החכמה בבינה,
phrases.en: to bring in new *chiddushim*, to bring in new ideas from the light of *chachma* into *bina*.
and this is what's called *ma'amik*, that it causes to deepen.
that it activates,
because it activates the depth of *chachma* and *bina* and causes them to come out and open up.

blocks.text: However, it is not so. Through the *iyun* of *bina* you are able to reach not only *chachma* but the depth of *chachma*, all the way to the inner *Keser*. Because **the depth of understanding, which is called the shaar hanun of bina** (the fiftieth gate), **even though it goes from the abstract point of chachma to be a yesh**, and you are now seeing only how the *chachma* was applied in this example, **its source reaches all the way up to the depth of chachma that he mentioned before.** It is true that you understand the depth only as it is in this example, but nevertheless that is the depth itself, the actual point. It may be only one example of it, but it has the whole *etzem* there. On the level of the *shaar hanun* it opens up all the way to the *etzem*, into the *chachma* and all the way up to the *Keser*.

We will explain the *shaar hanun* later, but the basic idea is this. In *Sefiras HaOmer* (the counting of the Omer) we count *chesed*, *chesed* of *chesed* and so on: we are counting the *middos* of *bina*. The fiftieth day, *Shavuos*, is the depth of *bina* itself, the *shaar hanun*, the *Keser*, *chachma* and *bina* of *bina*, the source of the *middos*. When you get that, you really get the *etzem* of the idea, which is higher than explaining or applying, and that is why we do not count the fiftieth day: it just comes down from above once you do your work. Your work is to do *hisbonenus*, to study the *middos*; say, in *halacha* (Jewish law), to study the laws, what is kosher and what is unfit. When you know all of that clearly, which is like the *middos*, then automatically you will have the *mochin* (the intellectual faculties) of why this is yes and this is no, which is the depth, and that includes all the way up to the real *etzem* of the idea.

Now the parentheses: like a wellspring going out. When *Moshiach* comes, **a wellspring is gonna go out from the Kodesh HaKodashim** (the Holy of Holies). **It's gonna start out very thin and narrow, like the horns of a grasshopper**, and then it will spread out, first like a string and then a thicker string, until eventually it is like a rushing river, as wide as a river. What is the idea? The *Kodesh HaKodashim* represents the *Keser*, the source, where the *etzem* is revealed. The wellspring represents *chachma*, and the river represents *bina*. Both the river and the wellspring come from the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, from the same place. The only difference is that the *chachma* stays in the source and the river goes out from it, but it is the same water, coming from the same place.

So even though the depth of *bina* leaves the source and is applied only in a particular example, the *etzem* is *mamash* there; that is just how the *etzem* is in this example. So when you understand it in this example, you really understand it in every example. You just have to learn to uncover what is external, what can change, what is just a garment, and what is the real *etzem*. Once you really find that *etzem*, it is the same for everything else. That is how you are able to get the idea.

blocks.title: The same water, traced back to the aquifer
blocks.text: So **its source reaches all the way up to the depth of chachma.** If you take the river and trace it up to its source, it comes from the wellspring; and if you keep tracing its water, it goes down the wellspring, through the veins in the earth's crust, all the way down to the underground source, the aquifer. It is really the same water; the water in the wellspring just came to you, all the way down the mountain to where you are. So even though *bina* is very far from *chachma*, when you understand something in *bina*, even a little concrete, tangible explanation, an example, the entire *chachma* is really hidden in it, all the way to the depth of *chachma*, because you have a little bit of the essence. "It's the same water," even though it came out very far from the source. "Doesn't matter."

blocks.title: One taste of the chocolate bar
blocks.text: If you just taste one little example of a chocolate bar, you may not know all the different forms of it or all the different ways to use it, but you have the essence. You know what it is, you know what it tastes like, because that stays the same. All the external things can change, but that inner point, the *shaar hanun*, stays the same; it is the same in *chachma* and the same in the *Keser*.

On the contrary, when it comes into *bina*, that is where you can really get it, because it is very tangible. So what we are saying is that even though *chachma* is very far beyond *bina*, very abstract, and *bina* very concrete, the depth of *bina* reaches all the way up to the depth that is even higher than *chachma*, all the way to the *Keser*, the source of *chachma*. And therefore, as we said originally, this is what we were trying to explain: it is possible, through doing *iyun* and learning explanations, to get new *chachmos*, a *chiddush* in *chachma*, which means that you are activating the depth of *chachma*.

**And like we see tangibly**, anybody who just studies and goes deeper into the depth of the *musag* (the concept as grasped), into the explanation of whatever he is learning, taps into the source and root of the concept as it is all the way up in *chachma*, **to bring in new chiddushim, to bring in new ideas from the light of chachma into bina**: he will get a new understanding in it. **And this is what's called ma'amik, that it causes to deepen**, a causative form: **it activates the depth of chachma and bina and causes them to come out and open up.** But it is done in an indirect way. It is true that you cannot actively go to the depth of *chachma*; that is why he took the *mashal* of the *Kodesh HaKodashim*. You cannot just go into the *Kodesh HaKodashim*. But by working to understand the *bina* better, automatically you will bring out more and more from the *chachma*, all the way up to the *Keser*.

blocks.title: Kuntres Etz HaChaim: how to learn Gemara
blocks.text:
The Rebbe Rashab explains all this in relation to learning *Gemara* in *Kuntres Etz HaChaim*, chapters 26 to 30. He tells the *bochurim* (students) in *Tomchei Temimim* how to learn *Gemara*, and basically explains the same process of learning that chapters 1 and 2 here explain for learning *Chassidus* or contemplating G-dliness.

He says there that when you learn *Gemara* you should not try to make *chiddushim*, to come up with new explanations and novel approaches and make a whole *pilpul* (Talmudic debate). Rather, you should just try to understand very clearly what the *Gemara* is saying, which is the *bina*, the *hisbonenus*. The more clearly you understand it, automatically you will get *chiddushim* in how to explain it. Then, once you understand the basic *pshat* (plain meaning) clearly, if you have a good mind for it, you can go deeper and make *diyukim* (precise inferences) in the exact wording and order of the *Mishna*, and you will understand even deeper and get even deeper *chiddushim*.

blocks.text: These two steps, understanding the basic *pshat* very clearly and then going deeper to make these little *diyukim*, are like *bina* and like *ma'amik*. But in both your focus is just to understand very clearly what the *Gemara* is saying. He says you have to be very careful that you are not trying to make a *chiddush*, and that everything is true: a *pshat* or a *diyuk* has to be really compelling, definitely true according to what it says there. If you do that, you will have a very good understanding, and automatically you will get the *chiddushim*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text:
It is the same with anything: with scientists when they research something, the latest research in, "I don't know, medicine, and cars, and space ships," computers, it does not matter. To be successful they have to study what is known, the things we have now, and understand how they work very well. Then they will be able to tap into the *chachma* behind it and see how to make it better and make innovations.

But sometimes, especially in medicine and things like that, people start working for grants and want to come up with some new idea; or someone has to write a thesis for his PhD, so he has to come up with a *chiddush*, some new discovery. Sometimes that can lead to dishonesty, because the person is not just trying to understand; he can just try to invent something. If you are trying to invent something more than you are trying to make it true and really understand clearly what is going on, "that's not the way to do it." The way to do it is just to try to understand everything very clearly, and automatically all this will come.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: The fiftieth gate in one plus one
blocks.text: The truth is that when you understand even the simplest explanation of something, you really have the depth there that includes everything in that wisdom, all the way to its source, where it connects to other wisdom. When you learn that one plus one is two, even that smallest example, or for a little kid, one apple plus one apple is two apples, when a child understands that he really gets the entire depth of the *shaar hanun*, the fiftieth gate of *bina*, in a very small way. And that point really includes the whole *chachma* of mathematics, and even of many other things, where mathematics connects to other disciplines like music and art.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: One plus one is one: mathematics as a language
blocks.text: In this idea of one plus one is two, what lies at the depth is that you see two separate things as combining and forming a unit even though they are separate. There is one apple and another apple, and they are separate and stay separate, but you view them as being together and call them two apples instead of just saying, "I have this apple and I have that apple." You are making a unity between them: something outside of them connects them even though they stay separate.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text: This is the basis of the whole mathematics we use, because at essence mathematics is a language, a way of describing the world, and you could describe it differently. You could take one piece of clay and another piece of clay and stick them together into one big piece: you could call that one plus one is one. Or you could look at one apple and another apple and see no common denominator connecting them: there is this apple and that apple, "so, 1 1 1 1." No making them two, because they are different and separate; why should I view them as one thing? The mathematics we use is a certain level of relationship, where you see things as separate but something higher than them connects them.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.text:
If we trace this back up to its source, it is the level of *Echad* that we spoke about in chapters 10 and 11. There are *Yachid*, *Echad* and *Kadmon*. *Yachid* is where everything is completely one: at that level one plus one would be one. Then there is the level of *Echad*, where you see that they are different things, separate and staying separate, but nevertheless something connects them: you see everything in the world as separate things, but they are all revealing the one G-d, all part of His revelation. And *Kadmon* is where you see everything as just being separate, so you see each thing as unique and you cannot really count them.

That is why you are not supposed to count people: you are not supposed to view them just as a number, where you lose sight of their individuality. You are supposed to have them by name, not by number, because each person is a completely different world. You cannot just lump them together.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: Separate notes, one melody
blocks.text: That perspective of *Echad* is what allows us to have music too. The basis, at the real depth of music, is that you take these separate notes, completely separate, and we hear them as one flowing thing: we hear a theme, a melody. That is something in our minds. If our mind heard each note as a separate thing without connecting them, we would not hear music, just a bunch of separate notes. We hear a melody, a song, because our mind hears the notes as separate and hears their differences, and at the same time puts them together and sees the whole theme of how they all work together.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 14 finishes line 28 (w0-139) and goes on explaining it; line 29 is read only in class 15.

blocks.title: Brush strokes and pixels, one picture
blocks.text: The same with art. When we look at a painting or a picture, it is a bunch of separate little brush strokes, or pixels, and our mind sees the contrast of all the different colors, but it also puts them all together into a picture. "Now some people, I think," if they were born with certain problems with their vision, even if it is corrected later in life, their mind will not have the skill of putting things together properly, to see a picture as we see it or to have proper depth perception. There are a lot of tricks in converting images into pictures as we see them: your mind has to interpret them a lot, to organize them, to recognize the distinctions and at the same time group them into a whole picture that connects them.

sections.title: Be wise with understanding, understand with wisdom: the navon who reaches the Keser
sections.summary: *Chacham b'vina* (*Ayin Beis* of *SaG*) is a *chiddush* within the idea one studies, born of the *iyun* that is *bina sheb'bina*; the *Keser* of *bina* is the depth of the concept, rooted in the depth of *chachma*. *Havein b'chachma* (*SaG* of *Ayin Beis*) is the power of explanation within *chachma* itself: the *navon*, whom Moshe could not find, understands one thing from another because he reaches the *Keser* that joins *chachma* and *bina*.

phrases.en: based on this,
this that it says in *Sefer Yetzira*, that you should understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding,

blocks.text: Based on this, in this parenthesis he explains some more details of how *chachma* and *bina* work, and especially how in their source *chachma* and *bina* connect with the *Keser*. On the simple level, *chachma* of *bina* is lower than *bina* of *chachma*: it is a progression upward, *bina* of *bina*, then *chachma* of *bina*, then *Keser* of *bina*, then *bina* of *chachma*, *chachma* of *chachma*, then *Keser* of *chachma*. But now he will explain that really, the ability to have *bina* in *chachma* or *chachma* in *bina*, even just *chachma* of *bina*, even that combination on the lowest level, requires that in some way you reach all the way up to the *Keser* that is higher than both of them and connects them; otherwise you will not be able to join *chachma* and *bina*. So even just to have a *chiddush* in *bina* really means that you are activating the *Keser*, the source of *chachma*.

That is why, when you keep doing *iyun* in *bina* and getting *chiddushim* in *bina*, it starts to activate the ability to make real *chiddushim* in *chachma* too: in a way, the ability to make a *chiddush* in *bina* is higher than the *chachma* itself, than making the *chiddush* itself. This is what he just finished explaining before the parenthesis, that just doing the *iyun* into the *bina* opens up and activates the depth of *chachma* and *bina*; that is why it is called *ma'amik*. That is the connection to this parenthesis.

Based on this, what it says in *Sefer Yetzira* (the Book of Formation), **that you should understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding.** *Havein b'chachma*, understand with wisdom: from your *chachma* you should come to understand; when you get a *chiddush*, a new idea, you should understand other things from that *chachma*. *Vachacham b'vina*, be wise with understanding: within *bina* you should have *chachma*; you should use your understanding to make a *chiddush*.

phrases.en: it's explained in the *maamarim* of the Alter Rebbe that are called *Kesavim*,
*Ayin Beis* of *SaG* means *chachma* within *bina*, and that's *chacham b'vina*, be wise with understanding.

phrases.he: שהוא רק להבין דבר חידוש אחר מתוך המושג דבינה,
phrases.en: to make a *chiddush* just within this understanding of *bina*.

phrases.he: שזה אינו אלא על ידי בחינת העיון הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: The only way that you'll understand an idea clearly and be able to make a *chiddush*, a new way to explain it or a new way to understand it, is if you study it very very well, which is the idea of *iyun*,

phrases.he: שהוא המברר כל חלקיו על בוריו,
phrases.en: this *iyun* is what clarifies all of the parts, all the details of the idea.
this is what's called *bina sheb'bina*.

blocks.text: It is explained in the Alter Rebbe's *maamarim* that are called *Kesavim* that this is *Ayin Beis* of *SaG*: the Name of seventy-two and the Name of sixty-three. These are different Names of G-d, different ways of spelling the Name *Havaya*. When you spell out each of its letters, that is called a *milui* (the spelling out of a letter's name): instead of just writing a *yud*, you write *yud-vav-dalet*; that is the *milui* of the letter *yud*. Later he will explain all four of these Names and what they represent.

In short, one spelling, which corresponds to *chachma*, has a *gematria* (numerical value) of seventy-two, and another spelling has a numerical value of sixty-three, and that one corresponds to *bina*. So *Ayin Beis* of *SaG* means *chachma* within *bina*, and that is *chacham b'vina*, be wise with understanding. The Name *Ayin Beis* is spelled entirely with *yuds*: *yud-vav-dalet, hei-yud, vav-yud-vav, hei-yud*. The Name *SaG* is the same spelling with one *alef* replacing a *yud*, so it is nine less: *yud-vav-dalet, hei-yud, vav-alef-vav, hei-yud*, which equals sixty-three. Later he will explain why they correspond to *chachma* and *bina*.

*Chacham b'vina* is *chachma* within *bina*, and it means **to make a chiddush just within this understanding of bina.** Whatever you are learning, you make a *chiddush* within that. You are learning a piece of *Gemara*, you are learning the Rashi, you have a question, and you make a *chiddush* within that Rashi, in how to explain it. The only way you will understand an idea clearly and be able to make a *chiddush*, a new way to explain or understand it, is if you study it very, very well, which is the idea of *iyun*: you really analyze it. **This iyun is what clarifies all of the parts, all the details of the idea**, and it is called *bina sheb'bina* (*bina* within *bina*). The analysis is *bina sheb'bina*, and through it you come to *chachma sheb'bina* (*chachma* within *bina*), the ability to make a *chiddush* within that idea.

blocks.text: **And then afterwards you'll be able to bear out a new thing and find a new understanding, but only within this idea that you're learning**: not a completely new idea that has nothing to do with it, just a new way of explaining this, an innovation. **That's called chachma of bina**: just a *chiddush* within the *bina*. *Chachma* means a *chiddush*, and *bina* means it is within the understanding.

**But the Keser of bina, that's the depth of the understanding**, and its source reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma* mentioned before. So when you reach the *omek hamusag*, you are reaching all the way up to the source of *chachma* as well.

phrases.en: and then understand with wisdom, that's *bina* of *chachma*,
that's the name of 63 within the name of 72, or *bina* within *chachma*,

that you're able to explain the *chachma* in many ways.

phrases.en: but this is still higher than an actual understanding in *bina*.

blocks.text: **And then understand with wisdom, that's bina of chachma**: *SaG* of *Ayin Beis*, the Name of sixty-three within the Name of seventy-two, *bina* within *chachma*. **That's the power of explanation that's within chachma itself, that you're able to explain the chachma in many ways.** This is the level where you get a new idea, a *chachma*, you see the point of the idea, and you see how from that point you could explain it in many different ways and apply it to many different things. That is the power of explanation hidden within the *chachma*.

blocks.title: Seeing the whole thing before describing it
blocks.text: **But this is still higher than an actual understanding in bina.** It is not an actual explanation yet. You see the *etzem* of the idea, the whole picture in the *chachma*, the point, and you have the ability to explain that point in many ways and apply it to many things, but you have not actually brought out an explanation yet. It is like actually seeing something. When you look at something you see the whole thing, all of its details, and how you could focus on different parts of it and explain it in different ways. If I ask you to describe it to me, you can describe it in all different ways and just keep describing, because you see the whole thing. But right now, even though you see it and notice all the details and distinctions you could explain to me, you did not actually explain it; even to yourself you did not explain it.

phrases.en: and this that it says,
he didn't find *nevonim*, he didn't find people of this type of understanding.

blocks.title: Moshe could not find nevonim
blocks.text: And this that it says, *nevonim lo ishtakchu*: when Moshe Rabbeinu was looking for judges, Yisro, his father-in-law, told him to find *nevonim*, people of superior understanding. But it says that Moshe found people with a lot of the qualifications, "he gave him I think seven qualifications," but he did not find *nevonim*, people of this type of understanding. Seemingly, there are a lot of very wise and talented people. Why could he not find a *navon*? What is such a big deal about a *navon*?

The idea of a *navon* is that **a navon is somebody that can understand one thing from something else.** What is so hard about that? It seems like just making a logical deduction. No, it is not just making a logical deduction. It is understanding one thing until you find its point, so that you see how the point of this idea explains something that seems completely different and unrelated, and you find the point that connects them. From one thing you understand, you can go all the way in, find its point and source, and understand something completely different.

This is like what the Arizal says, that somebody who knows how to make a *yichud* (union) can know whatever he wants to know: you can trace an idea all the way up to its source in the *Keser* and bring it back down into any other *chachma* you want, and from the *chachma* into any *bina* you want. That is the ability of a *navon*: to take an idea all the way up to the *Keser* and bring it all the way back down to the *bina*. At will you can go from *bina* to *chachma*, and from the *chachma* to any other *bina* you want; you can always find the abstract point that unites everything and bring it back and apply it to anything practical. To be free to move from *bina* to *chachma* and *chachma* to *bina* like that, you have to be a master of *chachma* and *bina*, which means that you reach the *Keser* that connects them both.

phrases.he: היינו מצד שרש כח זה דהבן בחכמה שמגיע בעומק דחכמה הנזכר לעיל,

phrases.en: And therefore you're able to take one idea, one *chachma*, and understand from it a completely different idea, a completely different subject.

blocks.text: The reason this is such a special thing is that **the ability to do this comes from the omek of chachma, from the depth of chachma, which is the Keser.** **And therefore you're able to take one idea, one chachma, and understand from it a completely different idea, a completely different subject.** From music you could understand math, or from math music; you could apply math to law, or law to psychology, or to physics. You just see how these seemingly unrelated things really connect. Or in the *Gemara*, from one *sugya* (topic) you are learning, say in *Gittin*, you could apply it to *Nezikin*, even though they seem totally unrelated.

blocks.text: **Which this is much higher than a chacham, from just the ability to get a chiddush**, to understand some new idea, which does not understand from it a different *sechel* (intellect). A regular *chacham* (wise man), when he gets an idea, gets a *chiddush*: a flash comes in, so good, he gets it. "But he's stuck." If he did not get a *chiddush* in something else, that is it; he only got the *chachma*, a flash of *chachma* in whatever he got it in. But a *navon* can take whatever he understands and from it understand anything else he wants to understand.

blocks.title: Two money changers
blocks.text: This is what Rashi says when he explains the difference between a *navon* and a *chacham*. One of the sages of the *Gemara* was asked by a Christian, Arius, "the Rebbe has a sicha about it": what is the difference between a *navon* and a *chacham*? He explained it with a *mashal*, which Rashi brings: two money changers. One is rich and one is an entrepreneur. The rich one sits there; when he gets business, he gets business, and when he does not, he just waits. The other is a go-getter: when he has business, he has business, and when he does not, he goes knocking on people's doors and getting business.

That is the difference. A *chacham* sits and learns, and if a *chiddush* comes to him, it comes to him; if it does not come, there is nothing he can do. The *navon*, when he is sitting and learning and gets a *chiddush*, gets a *chiddush*; and when he does not get it, he is able to go get it. Whenever he wants to understand something, he can go find it. The ability to do that means he reaches all the way up to the *Keser* and can bring out the *chachma* at will. That is the advantage of a *navon*.

phrases.he: (ומכל מקום מה שבהשגה דבינה מבין השגה חדשה מתוך ההשגה זו,
phrases.en: the ability to get a *chiddush* within even the same *hasaga*,
the source of that ability comes from *havein b'chachma*,
because that's already like a thing of understanding one thing from something else,

blocks.text: Now another parenthesis. Nevertheless, **the ability to get a chiddush within even the same hasaga** (comprehension), which is the *chachma* of *bina*, a much lower level of *chachma*, has its source in *havein b'chachma*, understanding with wisdom, because that is already a matter of understanding one thing from something else. It is just that you understand one thing from another within the *bina*, within the same thing you are learning. But it really comes from that ability to find the *chachma* and apply it from one thing to something else. The only difference is that *chachma* of *bina* is in a revealed *sechel*, and *bina* of *chachma*, the power of *havein b'chachma*, is in the source of the *sechel* in *chachma*, not in the revealed understanding of *bina*.

sections.title: The order of the levels: bina sheb'bina, chachma sheb'bina, Keser of bina
sections.summary: In sum: *iyun* is *bina sheb'bina*, sharp distinctions, from which comes length but not yet breadth; *chachma sheb'bina*, new explanations within the one idea, is breadth; and how long and broad an understanding can be depends on the depth of the concept, the *Keser* of *bina*.

Now he gives a little *kitzur* (summary) to sum up everything we have been saying.

It is not confused with something else, it is not blurry. Everything is very sharp and clearly defined: that is *bina* of *bina*.

That is called the width, because then you have a lot of explanations.
