sections.title: Daas is the bond of feeling, not the learning itself; its length, breadth and depth
sections.summary: What people call *ha'amakas hadaas* is not the delving itself, which is *hisbonenus*; *daas* is binding one's feeling to the concept, the caring that drives the *iyun* deeper. *Daas* too is long or short, broad or narrow, strong or light, and a light *daas*, like a child's, lacks depth and is easily turned to the opposite.

phrases.en: based on what we explained until now,
this that the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas*, deepening your *daas*,
this is not actually the delving into an idea.
like reaching the *omek hamusag* of *bina*.
for this learning process has no connection to *daas*.

blocks.text: **Based on what we explained until now, this that the world calls ha'amakas hadaas, deepening your daas**, is not the actual learning process; **this is not actually the delving into an idea.** *Ha'amakas hadaas* does not bring you deeper into the understanding of the idea. Based on what we explained, that is accomplished through *hisbonenus*. First of all, that is what brings you to the *omek hamusag*, the depth of *bina*, and it even brings you all the way up to *chachma*, to the depth of *chachma*, and brings you *chiddushim*. All those things of understanding, even to the highest level, and even bringing it all the way back to *bina*, being a *mevin* (one who understands), depend on *hisbonenus*, not on *ha'amakas hadaas*.

So *ha'amakas hadaas* is definitely not the actual learning process, **like reaching the omek hamusag of bina.** When you say you are going deeper into the idea, going from the outside of *bina* to the depth of *bina* to get the *omek hamusag*, that is not what we mean by *ha'amakas hadaas*, **for this learning process has no connection to daas.** So what is *daas*? Now he explains.

phrases.he: אך הדעת הוא בחינת התקשרות הרגשתו במושג ביותר,
phrases.en: *Daas* means to connect your feeling very deeply to the idea that you understand.

phrases.he: והוא שמביא לידי בחינת העמקה במושג,
phrases.en: this is what causes you to study the idea deeper
after you did the initial *iyun*.

phrases.he: שהוא רק כמו בחינת כלי לעומק ההשגה כנזכר לעיל.
phrases.en: So this *ha'amakas hadaas* is only a tool,

blocks.text: **Daas means to connect your feeling very deeply to the idea that you understand**: to feel a very deep personal relevance, to really connect to it, associate with it, sympathize with it, any kind of way of being very sensitive to the idea, emotionally, so that you feel it is connected to you and relevant to you.

blocks.title: The chicken story again
blocks.text: As this *HaYom Yom* says, the main thing for understanding *Chassidus* is to have a *daas* for it: if you feel it is personally relevant to you, you will understand, even something very difficult intellectually. He brings the example from the *Gemara* of the discussion Rabbi Meir ("I think it was Rabbi Meir") brought up in the *beis midrash* about a chicken. He kept bringing all these genius arguments to make it kosher, and they said, "Listen, Rabbi Meir, it's not kosher, just leave it." And he said, "All of these arguments were said to me by a simple peasant woman," who would not normally be coming up with such arguments, but since it was her chicken and it really bothered her, she was able to make arguments that the *Tannaim* and *Amoraim* would be discussing, though they were much more advanced in Talmudic law.
blocks.outOfPlace: The chicken story was first told in class 12, at line 21; here it is retold for its point about daas.

blocks.text: The example shows that if there is a will, there is a way: if you really feel it is important to you, you will understand. That is why *daas* is important. Not because it actually makes you understand, but because it makes you care, and if you care, you will do the *hisbonenus* automatically, and you will understand.

And this *ha'amakas hadaas*, this deep personal relevance you feel to the idea, **is what causes you to study the idea deeper after you did the initial iyun.** After you just learned the basics and got them clear, what is going to make you really push your mind to think about the idea more deeply, to bring up *chiddushim* and get the depth of *chachma* and everything like that? You need the motivation for that.

blocks.title: Passing the test, and free time
blocks.text: If you are in school and just learning something, you will do your *iyun*, memorize the material, and that is it; you will pass your test. That just requires *iyun*. But to go past that and start making *chiddushim*, you have to be interested in it; it is something you are going to do in your free time, something you really care about. You cannot be made to do that for a test, really.

**So this ha'amakas hadaas is only a tool**, a way of getting yourself to activate, to influence yourself to use your *bina* to analyze more deeply, which will give you the depth of understanding. It does not bring the depth of understanding itself; it is just a means to get you to study more deeply so that you understand more deeply. "So that's the idea of ha'amakas hadaas."

phrases.he: וגם בדעת יש אורך ורוחב ועומק,
phrases.en: *Daas* also has a length, width, and a depth.
for example, some people have a short *daas*, like a short attention span.
and some people have a long attention span.
and there are some people that have a broad, a wide *daas*, but it's not long.
like somebody who has a strong *daas*,

phrases.he: או דעת קל כנשים שדעתן קלות,
phrases.en: or a light *daas*, like women,
that means that the *daas* is not so deep.
and automatically, if the *daas* isn't so deep, it's also not so long and it's not so wide.

blocks.text: Now he explains how *daas* too has a depth, length and width. This is important because, as we have been saying, through studying the length and the width you get the depth. Suppose a person says, "Well, I don't have a deep *daas* for *Chassidus*. So that's it, what can I do? I learned it, and I know the basic thing, but I don't feel that it's personally relevant to me, and so I don't pursue it further than that." Just as, to get the *omek hamusag*, you study the length and the width of the explanations and automatically you get the depth, so too with *daas*: if you work on the length and width of *daas*, automatically you will get the depth of *daas*. And when you have a deep *daas*, which is the idea of *ha'amakas hadaas*, of working to deepen your connection, it will motivate you to study more and go more deeply in your understanding. "All right, should we delve into it?"

**Daas also has a length, width, and a depth.** **For example, some people have a short daas, like a short attention span, and some people have a long attention span.** That is one idea of the length of *daas*: how long you are able to sit on the idea. The other idea of the length of *daas*, as Reb Hillel explains, is wanting to bring the idea into a lot of *osios* (letters), to bring it down into letters. If you have a long *daas*, you want to bring it into a lot of *osios*.

That means you will want to sit and hear it for a long time, and talk about it for a long time, but it also means "you'll want to get a t-shirt, and a hat, and a bumper sticker." Those are also a lot of *osios*: bringing it down into physical things, "like paraphernalia." **And there are some people that have a broad, a wide daas, but it's not long**: it comes out in a lot of things, but it does not come down so far. The longer the *daas*, the more it comes down into physical paraphernalia like the t-shirt and the bumper sticker. If it is not so long, it stays in the book; they will discuss it as an intellectual thing, but they will not bring it down into physical *osios*.

blocks.title: "That reminds me of golf"
blocks.text: Somebody with a wide *daas* for a thing will talk about it a lot, from all different angles, and bring it up in all different parts of the day. That is width: it is connected to all different things, not just one thing. But maybe it is not long, so it is just something they discuss. Whatever subject comes up, they will be like, "Oh yeah, you know, that reminds me of golf." They are always talking about golf. That means they have a wide *daas* for it, especially if they know all about it. Knowing all about it shows they are interested; the knowledge itself is the *bina*, but the fact that they connect it to all different parts of their life is a wide *daas*.

Another thing in a wide *daas* is that you can handle two opposite things at once: you can see both sides of an argument. A narrow *daas* means that someone is interested in something, say politics, but only in the Republican side; he is interested only in a narrow aspect of politics. The same in *Chassidus*: if a person is interested only in *avoda'dike maamarim* (discourses on divine service), or only in *haskala'dike maamarim* (discourses of intellectual explanation), that is a narrow *daas*. Or someone interested only in the discourses of a certain Rebbe, or only in *maamarim* and not in *sichos*, letters or stories: if somebody is interested only in one aspect, that is a narrow *daas*.

sensitivity.reason: Names one party ("only in the Republican side") as the example of a narrow daas, which a reader may take as a partisan jab.
sensitivity.publishable: Another thing in a wide *daas* is that you can handle two opposite things at once: you can see both sides of an argument. A narrow *daas* means that someone is interested in something, say politics, but only in one side of it; he is interested only in a narrow aspect of politics. The same in *Chassidus*: if a person is interested only in *avoda'dike maamarim* (discourses on divine service), or only in *haskala'dike maamarim* (discourses of intellectual explanation), that is a narrow *daas*. Or someone interested only in the discourses of a certain Rebbe, or only in *maamarim* and not in *sichos*, letters or stories: if somebody is interested only in one aspect, that is a narrow *daas*.

blocks.text: A wide *daas* means that they do not see the two things as contradicting; they can handle both, because they are interested in something higher, something deeper. As we explained before, the length and width come from the depth: the deeper the source, the wider and longer it will be, because they do not see it as contradicting. If somebody were interested in the real depth of politics itself and the issues, he would be interested in both sides. The same if a person is really interested in *Chassidus* itself.

**Like somebody who has a strong daas**: when he connects to something, he gets totally engrossed in it and very firmly connected to it, and it is very hard to change his opinion about it. He will not get distracted; he will be totally engrossed in it for hours or days or years, and that is it. If he made up his mind, that is it: he is connected to this, this is the way he sees things, this is the way he feels things. That is the idea of a strong *daas*.

**Or a light daas, like women**: women are very good at multitasking. "Usually women are much better at that than men," and the reason is that usually women have a lighter *daas*: they do not get so engrossed in one thing. Also, men are usually stronger about their opinion: they get one thing and that is very, very firm, and women are a little bit more flexible. That is the idea of a *daas kal* (a light *daas*).

sensitivity.reason: In his own voice, past the line's words, generalizes that women are better at multitasking than men because their daas is lighter, and that men hold their opinions more firmly than women.
sensitivity.publishable: A light *daas* is one that does not get so engrossed in any one thing: such a person is good at doing several things at once, and more flexible, while a strong *daas* holds very firmly to one thing and one opinion. That is the idea of a *daas kal* (a light *daas*).

blocks.text: Although sometimes a *daas kal* can also mean *temimus'dik* (innocent, wholehearted), because it explains that a light *daas* also means you have only one *kav* (measure). That is the idea of a *tam* (a simple, wholehearted person): it says a *tam* has only one *kav* of *daas*. That means he cannot lie or be sneaky so much. If you are supposed to be nice, then he is being nice, and that is it; he cannot feel that he is supposed to be nice and at the same time act mean.

"It's harder for women to do that." It is not really a personal thing of which you would say, "I really have a strong feeling for it, a strong connection to it."

**Or a light daas, like women** whose *daas* is light. What does it mean that a *daas* is light? **That means that the daas is not so deep. And automatically, if the daas isn't so deep, it's also not so long and it's not so wide.**

"Men tend to connect much deeper to whatever they're doing and get much more engrossed in it," and automatically they become more obsessed with it, and it takes over everything in their life; and women tend not to do that as much.

sections.title: Daas focuses, bina spreads out: both together, to the root of chachma and bina
sections.summary: *Iyun* pauses on each point but at once spreads out into a broad picture; *daas* only gathers all the mind onto this one idea, the opposite of spreading. Yet it is *daas*, interest in the right place, that carries the *iyun* to the depths of *chachma* and *bina*: *daas* is hidden in *bina*, and Moshe, who was *daas*, merited the fiftieth gate.

phrases.en: which the *iyun* of *bina* itself is really the opposite of this idea of focusing and limiting yourself to just one idea.

blocks.text: **Which the iyun of bina itself is really the opposite of this idea of focusing and limiting yourself to just one idea.** *Daas* means you get fixated on one idea. But *bina* means you want to take the idea, pull it apart, see all of its parts, compare and contrast them, and see how they work together. For **even though when a person is doing iyun in bina, they dwell on each thing and they hold themselves back to spend time focusing on each point at first**, not going on to the next one until they have understood this one well, **immediately it starts to expand**, to grow more and more, and you start to put together a whole broad picture of all the different details: there is this and there is that, and they work together like this, and there is a third thing and a fourth thing, and you start to see how they all fit together.

Like what we are learning here. First you learn about *bina*, and *chachma*, and then *daas*. At first, learning about *bina*, we dwell on it; then we move on to *chachma* and dwell on that; and now we are on *daas* and dwell on that. And we are getting a bigger and bigger picture. That is the whole point of *bina*: to understand all the points and how they work together.

blocks.title: The watchmaker and the detective
blocks.text: Like a watchmaker taking a watch apart to examine it and fix it. First he takes it apart and looks at each piece carefully under a microscope, "not a microscope, a magnifying glass," to see if it is broken and examine its quality. He spends a lot of time on each part, but he is really trying to evaluate all of them and get a big picture: how he can put it back together and fix it, what could be wrong with it. Or a detective looking for clues: he may spend a lot of time on each detail, but he is trying to put together a big picture to figure out what happened. He does not just want to focus on each little detail. And yet he has to have a very big interest in the details; if he is not interested enough in the details to spend the time to really focus on them, he is not going to do a proper analysis.

So *daas* is not a process of thinking. It is not a cognitive, understanding process; it is not a learning process. What it is, is the focus that motivates you to really learn and really do the proper analysis.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן הצמצום והכיווץ דהעמקת הדעת,

blocks.text: **On the other hand, the focus and limiting of ha'amakas hadaas, of having a deep daas for something, really connecting to the idea**, is, on the contrary, only the focus: gathering all the power of the mind to connect only to this concept. **The whole idea of daas is only the focus.** The whole *daas* does not try to build a big picture. It is that you are very interested and very focused on what you are doing right now and totally engrossed in it. You totally put yourself into it. You do not hear anything, you do not see anything; you get totally into it.

There are stories of people who, when they were *davenen* or learning, would not even hear or know what was going on around them. That sounds like a very deep level of *daas*, not something for a regular person, to be that much into what he is doing. But really it is very easy for anybody; they just have to be interested. If you just develop an interest in what you are doing, automatically you will have a very strong *daas* for it, a very strong concentration and focus on it.

blocks.title: The kid in front of the video
blocks.text: You see this: take any kid, stick him in front of a TV, a video or something like that, "and bam, they're out. They don't see you, they don't hear you, they don't know nothing." So you see it is just a matter of how connected you are to the thing. With a video it is easy, because there you have all this stuff going on, pictures that are moving and sounds and music; it is very captivating. But when you start to learn something and develop an interest in it through doing *iyun*, through studying an idea, and your *daas* starts to connect to it, you start to focus on that idea a lot and become very engrossed in it and very, very connected to the idea.

phrases.he: שזה היפך בחינת התפשטות העיון בהרחבת ענין המושכל,
phrases.en: this is the opposite of the way that *iyun* takes an idea and it tries to spread it out and get a broad picture of the idea.

phrases.en: means when you grasp an idea and it really settles into you very well.

phrases.he: ואמנם על ידי העמקת הדעת בא לידי עמקות המושכל עד שרשו בעמקי החכמה ובינה
phrases.en: it's this interest that causes your *iyun* to keep going deeper and deeper into the idea, which will bring you eventually to the depth of *chachma* and *bina*.

blocks.text: This focus on the idea, getting totally engrossed in what you are doing right now and forgetting about everything else that exists, **is the opposite of the way that iyun takes an idea and it tries to spread it out and get a broad picture of the idea.** When you are learning, you do not just want to know this one little thing you are learning right now; you want to know the whole thing. If you are learning *halacha*, you do not just want to know this one law, you want to know all the laws: you want to know the laws of *Shabbos*, everything about *Shabbos*, what to do. You want the whole picture. But right now you are learning one law, and you have to totally focus on whatever you are doing right now. If you do not have the *daas* to totally focus and concentrate on it and not think about everything else, you will not really analyze it properly and really understand it. But then you have to keep moving from point to point, and step back and see how they fit together too.

blocks.text: So you need both together, and when you are learning you have to have the right balance between how much you go in depth and how much you force yourself to go on and put together the picture. That is why *chazara* (review) is a very good thing: it lets you focus on each thing you learn, and at the same time forces you to go on and build a big picture, which also helps you understand. And then you can always come back and, using everything you have learned, go deeper and understand it better; and then go through it all again, and come back and do it deeper and better. That way you have a balance of the two. If you just learn one thing until you understand it perfectly, you could really go forever, because there is always deeper to go. So you have to have that balance of *daas* and *bina*: you focus on what you are doing and stop to focus on this until you understand it, and on the other hand you learn to move on and keep building the whole picture.

One more thing about this difference between *bina* and *daas*. In *daas* you are not focusing because you want to understand. *Daas* is focusing because you like this idea, you are really connected to it, really interested in it. *Daas* is just that you like where you are now and want to stay there; you want to savor it and stay with it, because you enjoy it. *Bina* is after a goal: you want to understand, so it wants you to go on too. So the *bina* is really what will make you understand; but if you do not have a *daas*, you will not use your *bina* enough, and then it will not accomplish what it was supposed to accomplish.

In Yiddish, *der klep mit dem arainleigen zich gor*: when you grasp an idea and it really settles into you very well. So yes, *amkus hadaas* is the opposite of this breadth of *bina*: you are totally preoccupied and you totally put yourself into it. And yet, through *amkus hadaas* one comes to the depth of the concept, to its root in the depths of *chachma* and *bina*. Even though *daas* is the opposite of *bina*, you need the *daas* to connect your *iyun* so that you will be *me'ayen* (analyzing) in the right place. **It's this interest that causes your iyun to keep going deeper and deeper into the idea, which will bring you eventually to the depth of chachma and bina.** Without the *daas* you will only analyze the external idea and understand only the external idea. So it is important: the deeper your *daas* is, it is basically like knowing what you are after. The more you know what you are after and connect your interest in the right place, the better you understand.

This is like what it says: one who learns in order to teach is given the means to learn and to teach. You would think, "It's hard enough for me to learn; if I'm going to teach, I'm not going to have time to learn." No: if you learn in order to teach, you will have time to learn and time to teach. And one who learns in order to do is given the means to learn and to teach, to keep and to do: if you learn in order to bring it into action, to live it, you will have time to learn and to teach and to guard and to do.

Why? Because the reason you are learning, where your interest lies, is your *daas*. And the deeper into the essence of the idea you connect your *daas*, the easier it is for your *iyun* to go in the right place, and you will find the depth. The real depth of the Torah is that it is not just for you: you want to bring it to other people too, and not just to other people in learning; you want to bring it to action. When you learn in order to bring it to action, that is where you are really getting the essence of the Torah, and then you understand much more quickly, because you are looking in the right place. You are analyzing from the Torah's point of view, you see what it is after, everything fits into place, and you get the depth. But if you do not go after the *etzem*, the essence, the depth, you will not get the depth. "So if you just learn to like, you know, know esoteric, you know, babble, then you'll know esoteric babble, that's it."

This inner interest means that when you study, you will not only get the depth of *bina* but also start to bring out *chiddushim*, because the more you connect yourself to it, the more you apply yourself to it, the more successful you will be in what you are doing. When you really apply yourself, you start to connect your *koach hamaskil*, your source of new ideas and ingenuity, to it, and you start to bring out *chiddushim*, new ideas in your understanding.

**And this is what it says that daas is hidden in the mouth of the mother.** Hidden in the ability to understand is really that there was a deep interest. The *Ima* (mother) represents *bina*, understanding. Externally *bina* looks like the opposite of *daas*; it looks as if it does not have so much *daas*. But really, hidden behind it is a very deep *daas*, and that is what gives the ability to understand.

blocks.text: **Like it says**, Moshe, who is *daas*, merited *bina*. Moshe was *daas*: his soul level was the level of *daas*, he had a very deep connection to everything, a very deep interest in everything, so he merited *bina*, to understand everything: **which that's the 50th gate of bina**, the *shaar hanun*, the inner depth of *bina*, which reaches all the way up to the *Keser*, as we explained before.

**Because the two are interdependent**: *chachma* and *bina* have to go and come together. As it says in *Pirkei Avos*, "If there is no *daas* there is no *bina*; if there is no *bina* there is no *daas*." You cannot have one without the other. **Like it's explained in many places in the Kesavim**, the Chassidic manuscripts, the long *maamarim* of the Alter Rebbe. **And that is enough for a mevin to understand.**
